Neuron.q: A scientist looks at a single cell that sends signals through the nervous system. What is she looking at?
wrong: A glial cell that only supports other cells
Glia support and protect neurons; they aren't the signaling cell.
A hormone is a chemical, not a cell.
That is the chemical messenger a neuron releases.
Neuron.exp: Neurons are the basic building blocks of the nervous system.

Glial cells (glia).q: Which cells outnumber neurons and spend their time nourishing and protecting them?
wrong: Those carry messages; they don't mainly support other cells.
Vesicles are sacs inside neurons, not cells.
Glial cells (glia).exp: Glia = glue: they support the system.

Dendrites.q: A neuron receives a chemical message from the neuron next to it. Which part detects the message first?
wrong: The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body.
The terminal buttons at the very end of the axon
Those send signals on, not receive them.
Myelin coats and speeds up the axon.

Soma.q: Which part of the neuron holds the nucleus and decides whether the neuron will fire?
wrong: The dendrites that receive chemical messages
Dendrites receive signals; the soma decides.
That is the gap between neurons.
Soma.exp: The soma is the cell body.

Axon.q: Once a neuron fires, which part does the electrical impulse travel down?
wrong: Dendrites receive; the impulse travels down the axon.
The synapse is a gap, not a pathway inside the neuron.
The soma starts the signal; it travels down the axon.
Axon.exp: Axon = away from the cell body.

Myelin sheath.q: Two neurons are identical except that one has a fatty coating on its axon. What will be different?
wrong: It will release fewer neurotransmitters into the synapse
Myelin affects speed, not how much is released.
Myelin sheath.exp: Myelin protects the axon and speeds the signal, like insulation on a wire.

Terminal branches.q: After traveling down the axon, the signal spreads into the frayed ends of the axon. What are these ends called?
wrong: Dendrites are at the receiving end, not the end of the axon.
The soma is the cell body.
Terminal branches.exp: Terminal branches are the axon's frayed ends, each ending in a terminal button.

Terminal buttons.q: Where are the vesicles of neurotransmitters held, at the tip of each terminal branch?
wrong: In the myelin sheath along the length of the axon
Myelin is a fatty coating, not storage.
The synapse is the gap they are released into.
Terminal buttons.exp: Terminal buttons are knobs that hold the vesicles.

Vesicles.q: A drug damages the tiny sacs that store neurotransmitters. Which part is it damaging?
wrong: The receptor sites on the next neuron's dendrites
The soma is the cell body.
Vesicles.exp: Vesicles store neurotransmitters in the terminal buttons.

Synapse.q: Neurotransmitters are released and float across to the next neuron. What space do they cross?
wrong: The myelin sheath around the axon
Myelin is a coating, not a gap.
The axon is part of the neuron.
Synapse.exp: The synapse is the gap; neurons never actually touch.

Resting potential.q: A neuron isn't firing; its dendrites are just waiting to receive neurotransmitters. What state is it in?
wrong: The refractory period after it has just fired
That is the level needed to fire.

Threshold.q: A neuron gets a little stimulation and doesn't fire, then more and it does. What level did the stimulation finally reach?
wrong: That is recovery time after firing.
Resting potential, the state of not firing
That is the state before firing.
Threshold.exp: The neuron fires only once threshold is reached.

Action potential.q: Threshold is reached and an electrical signal races from the soma down the axon. What is this signal?
wrong: Reuptake of neurotransmitters into the sending neuron
Action potential.exp: The action potential is the neuron firing.

All-or-none principle.q: A doctor doubles the strength of a stimulus to a neuron that already fires. What happens to how strongly it fires?
All-or-none principle.right: Nothing; it fires the same way
wrong: It fires twice as strongly as before
A stronger stimulus never makes a stronger firing.
It either fires completely or not at all.
All-or-none principle.exp: All or none: a neuron fires completely or not at all.

Reuptake.q: After a message is sent, leftover neurotransmitters are pulled back into the neuron that released them. What is this?
wrong: That is recovery time when the neuron can't fire.
That is the level needed to fire.
An action potential traveling the axon

Refractory period.q: Right after firing, a neuron gets flooded with neurotransmitters but still can't fire. Why?
wrong: It's at resting potential, waiting for input
At rest it could fire if stimulated.
Myelin damage slows signals; it doesn't block firing right after a fire.
That would leave more neurotransmitter in the synapse.
Refractory period.exp: Like a toilet: you have to wait to flush again.

Multiple sclerosis (MS).q: A patient's axons are losing their fatty coating, and walking has become difficult. What is the most likely disease?
wrong: Myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune muscle disorder
That blocks acetylcholine receptors; it doesn't damage myelin.
That is linked to memory and low acetylcholine.
That is linked to low dopamine.

Myasthenia gravis.q: A patient's antibodies are destroying the muscles' receptor sites for acetylcholine, causing weakness. What disorder is this?
wrong: Multiple sclerosis, a breakdown of myelin
MS damages myelin, not acetylcholine receptors.
That is linked to low dopamine.
That is linked to high dopamine.
Myasthenia gravis.exp: An autoimmune disorder blocking acetylcholine receptors at the muscles.

Neurotransmitter.q: A chemical is released into the synapse and carries a signal to the next neuron. What is it?
wrong: A hormone carried through the bloodstream
Hormones travel in the blood, not across a synapse.
That is the sac that stores it.
Neurotransmitter.exp: Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers between neurons.

Excitatory.q: A chemical makes the next neuron more likely to fire. How is it described?
wrong: Inhibitory, because it calms the next neuron
Inhibitory keeps the next neuron from firing.
That is the recovery period, not a chemical type.
That describes neurons carrying sensory messages in.

Inhibitory.q: A chemical keeps the next neuron from firing. How is it described?
wrong: Excitatory, because it signals the neuron to go
That describes motor neurons carrying signals out.

Acetylcholine (ACh).q: A patient with Alzheimer's has trouble with memory, and a doctor suspects too little of a chemical that also controls muscle action. Which one?
wrong: Low dopamine is linked to Parkinson's.
Low serotonin is linked to depression.
Acetylcholine (ACh).exp: ACh controls movement and plays a role in memory; too little is linked to Alzheimer's.

Dopamine.q: A patient has tremors and trouble starting movements. Low levels of which neurotransmitter are most likely?
wrong: Glutamate is tied to thinking and learning; too much is linked to anxiety.
Too little GABA is linked to anxiety.
Dopamine.exp: Low dopamine is linked to Parkinson's.

Serotonin.q: A doctor treats a patient's depression with a drug that keeps more of a mood-related chemical in the synapse. Which chemical?
wrong: ACh is about movement and memory.
Serotonin.exp: Low serotonin is linked to depression; SSRIs raise it.

SSRI.q: A drug blocks the reabsorption of serotonin so it stays in the synapse longer. What kind of drug is it?
wrong: That would target dopamine, not serotonin.
SSRI.exp: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor: an antidepressant.

Norepinephrine.q: A neurotransmitter that also acts as a hormone sharpens focus and drives the fight-or-flight response. Which one?

GABA.q: A patient with an anxiety disorder may have too little of the brain's natural tranquilizer. Which chemical?
wrong: Too much glutamate, not too little, is linked to anxiety.
Dopamine is about reward and movement.
GABA.exp: GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter; too little is linked to anxiety.

Glutamate.q: A student is learning new vocabulary. Which major excitatory neurotransmitter is involved in thinking, memory and learning?
Glutamate.exp: Glutamate = go: the major excitatory neurotransmitter.

Endorphins.q: After a long run, Jamie feels a wave of calm and less pain. Which chemicals are responsible?
wrong: Substance P, which sends pain signals
Substance P sends pain signals; endorphins relieve pain.
Endorphins.exp: Endorphins are natural painkillers: the runner's high.

Substance P.q: Levels of a neurotransmitter rise when you touch a hot stove and feel pain. Which one?
wrong: Endorphins reduce pain; substance P sends it.

Three functions of the nervous system.q: You see a ball, decide to catch it, and move your hands. Which order of nervous system functions does this follow?
wrong: Motor output, integration, then sensory input at the very end
The senses come first, then the decision, then movement.
You must sense the ball before deciding.
The brain decides before you move.
Three functions of the nervous system.exp: Gather information, process it, act on it.

Sensory (afferent) neurons.q: Your finger touches a hot pan. Which neurons carry that message in to the spinal cord and brain?
wrong: Motor (efferent) neurons that run out to the muscles
Those relay between sensory and motor neurons.

Motor (efferent) neurons.q: After your brain decides to pull your hand back, which neurons carry the signal out to your arm muscles?
wrong: Sensory (afferent) neurons that run in from the skin
Those connect neurons inside the brain and spinal cord.

Interneurons.q: Which neurons inside the spinal cord connect the message from your skin to the signal going out to your muscles?
wrong: Sensory neurons carrying the message from the skin

Central nervous system (CNS).q: A car accident damages a person's spinal cord. Which division of the nervous system was injured?
wrong: The peripheral nervous system of nerves in the limbs
The spinal cord is central, not peripheral.
That is part of the peripheral system.
That is a system of glands.

Spinal cord.q: Which structure acts as the "highway" sending messages both ways between the brain and the body?
wrong: The corpus callosum, linking the two hemispheres
That connects the hemispheres, not brain to body.
Spinal cord.exp: The spinal cord connects the brain to the body.

Peripheral nervous system (PNS).q: Nerves in your hand are damaged, but your brain and spinal cord are fine. Which division was injured?
wrong: The central nervous system of brain and spinal cord
The brain and spinal cord are fine.
That is a group of brain structures.
Peripheral nervous system (PNS).exp: PNS = all nerves outside the brain and spinal cord.

Nerves.q: Bundles of neurons run like wires from your spinal cord to your fingers. What are these bundles called?
wrong: Glial cells packed around the spinal cord
Glia support neurons; they aren't bundles of them.
Those are chemicals in the blood.
Nerves.exp: Nerves carry messages to and from the CNS.

Somatic nervous system.q: You decide to pick up a pencil. Which part of the peripheral nervous system controls this?
wrong: The autonomic nervous system, which runs on its own
That controls involuntary actions like heartbeat.

Autonomic nervous system.q: Your heart beats and your stomach digests food without you thinking about it. Which system controls this?
wrong: The somatic nervous system of voluntary movement

Sympathetic nervous system.q: A dog suddenly lunges at you, and your heart pounds and you're ready to run. Which system is active?
Sympathetic nervous system.exp: Sympathetic = stressed: fight, flight or freeze.

Parasympathetic nervous system.q: After the dog leaves, your heart rate slows and you calm down. Which system is now active?

Reflex.q: A doctor taps your knee and your leg kicks before you even think about it. Why is this so fast?
Reflex.right: The spinal cord directs it, not the brain
wrong: The brain plans the kick in advance
Hormones carry the signal through the blood quickly
Reflexes are directed by the spinal cord.
Reflex.exp: Reflexes skip the brain, which makes them faster.

Endocrine system.q: Which system uses glands to release hormones into the bloodstream?
wrong: The somatic nervous system of voluntary movement
That is a group of brain structures.
That is the brain and spinal cord.
Endocrine system.exp: The endocrine system is the system of glands.

Hormones vs. neurotransmitters.q: Why does the jittery feeling after a scare last longer than the quick jolt of fear itself?
Hormones vs. neurotransmitters.right: Hormones in the blood act slower but last longer
wrong: Neurotransmitters travel through the blood very slowly
The difference is how hormones travel.
Hormones vs. neurotransmitters.exp: Hormones travel through the bloodstream: slower, but longer lasting.

Pituitary gland.q: Which gland signals the other glands to release their hormones?
wrong: The adrenal glands on top of the kidneys
That is a sensory relay station, not a gland.
Pituitary gland.exp: The pituitary is the master gland.

Adrenaline.q: During a scary roller coaster, your heart rate, blood pressure and blood sugar jump. Which hormone caused this?
Adrenaline.exp: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands fuels fight-or-flight.

Ghrelin.q: Your stomach growls before lunch. Which hormone is telling your body you're hungry?

Leptin.q: After Thanksgiving dinner you feel stuffed and push your plate away. Which hormone signals this?

Testosterone.q: Which sex hormone is most responsible for sex drive and, in excess, is linked to aggression?
Testosterone.exp: Testosterone: sex drive; too much is linked to aggression.

Estrogen.q: Which sex hormone, important for reproduction, do women have more of?
wrong: Testosterone, which men have more of

Oxytocin.q: A new mother feels a powerful bond with her baby during and after birth. Which hormone is most involved?
Oxytocin.exp: Oxytocin is the love or bonding hormone.

Melatonin.q: As it gets dark at night, you start feeling sleepy. Which hormone is rising?
wrong: That wakes you up for fight-or-flight.
Melatonin.exp: Melatonin from the pineal gland responds to darkness.

Brainstem.q: Which part of the brain, made of the medulla and pons, handles automatic survival functions?
wrong: The cerebral cortex, the wrinkled outer layer

Medulla.q: A blow to the base of the brainstem stops a person's breathing. Which structure was damaged?
Medulla.exp: The medulla controls breathing and heartbeat.

Pons.q: Which brainstem structure is especially involved in the sleep-wake cycle and connects the spinal cord to the brain?
wrong: The amygdala is in the limbic system.

Reticular formation.q: After damage to a network in the brainstem, a patient falls into a coma. Which network was damaged?
wrong: The corpus callosum between the hemispheres
Reticular formation.exp: The reticular formation controls arousal and consciousness.

Thalamus.q: Light, sound and touch signals are all routed through one structure on their way to the cortex. Which one?
wrong: That regulates hunger, thirst and temperature.
Thalamus.exp: The thalamus is the sensory switchboard (every sense but smell).

Cerebellum.q: After a few drinks, a person stumbles and can't walk a straight line. Which part of the brain is most affected?
wrong: The hippocampus, which stores long-term memory
Cerebellum.exp: The cerebellum handles balance and coordination; alcohol strongly affects it.

Limbic system.q: Which group of brain structures, including the amygdala and hippocampus, handles emotion and long-term memory?
wrong: The brainstem of the medulla and pons
That is the wrinkled outer layer.
That is a system of glands.

Amygdala.q: A woman with damage to one brain structure shows no fear, even of snakes. Which structure is most likely damaged?
Amygdala.exp: The amygdala processes fear and aggression.

Hippocampus.q: After surgery, a patient can't form any new long-term memories. Which structure was most likely removed?
Hippocampus.exp: A hippo never forgets: the hippocampus stores new long-term memories.

Hypothalamus.q: Which structure monitors body temperature, hunger, thirst and sexual responses?
wrong: The thalamus, the sensory relay station
Hypothalamus.exp: The hypothalamus: feeding, fighting, fleeing, mating.

Lateral hypothalamus (LH).q: A rat with damage to one part of its hypothalamus stops eating entirely. Which part?
wrong: The ventromedial hypothalamus, which signals fullness
Lateral hypothalamus (LH).exp: Lateral = lunch: damage means loss of hunger.

Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH).q: A rat with damage to one part of its hypothalamus overeats and never seems full. Which part?
wrong: The lateral hypothalamus, which triggers hunger
Damage there causes loss of hunger.
Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH).exp: Ventromedial = very full: damage means overeating.

Cerebral cortex.q: Which wrinkled outer layer of the brain is split into two hemispheres and four lobes?
wrong: The limbic system deep inside the brain
That is a group of inner structures.
That is the medulla and pons.
That is the "little brain" at the back.
Cerebral cortex.exp: Four lobes: frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal (F-POT).

Frontal lobe.q: Which lobe holds the prefrontal cortex, the motor cortex and Broca's area?
wrong: The temporal lobe, which holds Wernicke's area
Wernicke's area is in the temporal lobe.
Frontal lobe.exp: The frontal lobe is at the front of the brain.

Prefrontal cortex.q: A teen makes impulsive decisions partly because one area involved in judgment and planning isn't fully developed. Which area?
wrong: The somatosensory cortex, which registers touch
Prefrontal cortex.exp: The prefrontal cortex handles executive functions like judgment and planning.

Motor cortex.q: A stroke damages the strip at the back of a patient's frontal lobe, and he can't move his arm on purpose. Which area?
wrong: The somatosensory cortex just behind it
Motor cortex.exp: The motor cortex controls voluntary movement.

Broca's area.q: Which area in the left frontal lobe controls speech production?
wrong: Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe

Broca's aphasia.q: After a stroke, a man understands questions but can only answer "Walk... dog..." with great effort. What does he most likely have?
wrong: Wernicke's aphasia, where fluent speech makes little sense
In Wernicke's, speech flows but makes little sense.
Broca's aphasia.exp: Short, effortful sentences with good understanding = Broca's aphasia.

Phineas Gage.q: After an iron rod went through his prefrontal cortex, a man became irritable, profane and dishonest. What does his case show?
wrong: The cerebellum controls a person's balance and coordination
His change was in personality, not balance.
Phineas Gage.exp: Phineas Gage's personality changed after damage to his prefrontal cortex.

Parietal lobe.q: A patient loses the ability to feel temperature and pressure on her skin and struggles with spatial orientation. Which lobe is damaged?
wrong: The occipital lobe at the back of the brain
Parietal lobe.exp: The parietal lobe processes body sensations and spatial orientation.

Somatosensory cortex.q: Which strip, directly behind the motor cortex, registers touch and body sensations?
wrong: The motor cortex just in front of it
Somatosensory cortex.exp: M before S: motor cortex, then somatosensory cortex.

Temporal lobe.q: Which lobe, by your temples above your ears, processes hearing and stores long-term memories?
wrong: The parietal lobe on top of the brain
Temporal lobe.exp: Temporal = by your temples, near your ears.

Primary auditory cortex.q: A patient's ears work perfectly, but damage to one area of the temporal lobe leaves her unable to process sounds. Which area?
wrong: The somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe
Primary auditory cortex.exp: Hearing is processed in the primary auditory cortex.

Wernicke's area.q: Which temporal lobe area lets you understand spoken and written language?
wrong: Broca's area in the left frontal lobe
Wernicke's area.exp: Wernicke = words don't make sense when damaged.

Wernicke's aphasia.q: After a stroke, a woman speaks fluently but says, "The table is running the purple Tuesday." What does she most likely have?
wrong: Broca's aphasia, with short, effortful speech
In Broca's, speech is short and halting, not fluent nonsense.
That is how the brain controls the body.
That is the brain's ability to change.
Wernicke's aphasia.exp: Fluent speech that makes little sense = Wernicke's aphasia.

Occipital lobe.q: A soldier's eyes are unharmed, but an injury to the back of his brain leaves him blind. Which lobe was damaged?
wrong: The temporal lobe on the side of the brain

Corpus callosum.q: To stop severe seizures, surgeons cut the band connecting the two hemispheres. What did they cut?
wrong: The reticular formation in the brainstem
Corpus callosum.exp: The corpus callosum lets the hemispheres communicate.

Brain lateralization.q: Language is mostly handled by the left side of the brain and face recognition by the right. What does this show?
wrong: Neurogenesis, the growth of new neurons
Brain lateralization.exp: Some functions are specialized to one side of the brain.

Contralateral control.q: A stroke damages the right side of a patient's brain. Which side of the body is most likely affected?
wrong: The right side, the same side as the damage
Each side of the brain controls the opposite side.
Movement would be affected on the opposite side.

Left hemisphere.q: Damage to which hemisphere is most likely to affect speech, math and recognizing words?
wrong: The right hemisphere, which recognizes faces
The right handles faces, space and emotion.

Right hemisphere.q: A patient can still talk but can't recognize her family's faces or hear emotion in voices. Which hemisphere is most likely damaged?
wrong: The left hemisphere, which handles language
Her speech is fine; the left handles language.
Right hemisphere.exp: The right handles faces, emotion and tone of speech.

Plasticity.q: In a blind person who reads Braille, the sense of touch takes over parts of the visual cortex. What does this show?
wrong: Lateralization of language to the left hemisphere
Plasticity.exp: The brain can change and reorganize.

Neurogenesis.q: Why is brain damage often permanent, even though the brain can make some new neurons?
Neurogenesis.right: New neurons form in only two areas
wrong: Neurons can't send signals after the age of 25
Glial cells kill all new neurons
Neurogenesis.exp: Neurogenesis happens only in two areas (memory and smell).

EEG.q: A doctor puts electrodes on a patient's scalp to look for seizure activity in her brain waves. Which test is this?
wrong: A CT scan using X-rays of the brain's structure
A CT shows structure, not electrical activity.
An MRI uses magnets to show structure.

PET scan.q: Researchers inject radioactive glucose to see which brain regions are most active during a task. Which scan is this?
wrong: A CT scan of the brain's structure
A CT shows structure with X-rays.
An MRI shows structure with magnets.
PET scan.exp: PET shows where glucose is used, which regions are active.

CT scan.q: A doctor uses X-rays to check whether a patient has a brain tumor. Which scan is this?
wrong: An fMRI that measures blood flow
An fMRI shows function, not X-ray images.

MRI.q: A doctor wants a detailed picture of a patient's brain tissue using strong magnetic pulses. Which scan is this?
wrong: A PET scan using radioactive glucose
A PET shows activity with glucose.

fMRI.q: Researchers want to see which brain areas light up while people look at faces, by measuring blood flow and oxygen. Which scan?
wrong: A CT scan showing the brain's structure
A regular MRI shows structure, not function.
fMRI.exp: f = function: blood flow and oxygen use.

Cornea.q: Light from a lamp first passes through which clear, protective outer layer of the eye?
wrong: The retina at the back of the eye
The retina is the last stop, not the first.
Light reaches the lens after the cornea and pupil.
That carries signals to the brain.
Cornea.exp: The cornea is where light first enters.

Iris.q: An airport scanner identifies you by the colored muscle around your pupil. What is it scanning?
wrong: The retina's rods and cones in the back of the eye
The scanner reads the colored muscle, not the retina.
Iris.exp: The iris controls pupil size and is unique to you.

Pupil.q: In a dark movie theater, the small opening in your eye gets bigger to let in more light. What is it?
wrong: The lens, which changes shape to focus
The lens focuses; the pupil lets light in.
The cornea is a fixed outer layer.
Pupil.exp: The pupil is the adjustable opening.

Lens.q: Which transparent structure behind the pupil changes shape to focus images on the retina?
wrong: The cornea, the clear outer layer
The cornea protects; the lens changes shape to focus.
That carries signals to the brain.

Accommodation.q: You look up from your phone to a sign far away, and the sign comes into focus. What process happened?
wrong: Dark adaptation as your pupils widen in dim light
That converts light into neural impulses.
Accommodation.exp: The lens changes shape to focus on near or far objects.

Retina.q: Where in the eye are the rods and cones, and where is light turned into neural signals?
wrong: The cornea at the front of the eye
The cornea lets light in; it has no receptors.
Retina.exp: The retina is the light-sensitive surface where transduction happens.

Transduction.q: Light hits your retina and is turned into signals your brain can read. What is this conversion called?
wrong: Accommodation of the lens to focus the image
That happens later, in the brain.
Transduction.exp: Turning one form of energy into neural impulses.

Rods.q: On a moonlit hike, you can see shapes but not colors. Which receptors are doing most of the work?
wrong: Cones, which handle color and fine detail
Cones work poorly in dim light.
Those connect receptors to ganglion cells.
Rods.exp: Rods = reduced light, black and white.

Cones.q: Reading small colored print in bright light depends mostly on which receptors?
wrong: Rods, which work best in dim light
Rods don't see color or fine detail.
Those are in the visual cortex.

Dark adaptation.q: You walk into a dark room and can barely see, but about 20 minutes later you can make out the furniture. What happened?
wrong: Accommodation as the lens changes its shape
That is focusing, not adjusting to dark.
That always happens when light hits the retina.
That is one sense affecting another.
Dark adaptation.exp: Pupils dilate to let more light in; it takes about 20 minutes.

Bipolar cells.q: Which cells connect the rods and cones to the ganglion cells?
wrong: Feature detectors in the visual cortex
Those are in the brain, not the retina.

Ganglion cells.q: Whose axons bundle together to form the optic nerve?
wrong: Bipolar cells, next to the rods and cones
Bipolar cells connect receptors to ganglion cells.
Ganglion cells.exp: Ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve.

Optic nerve.q: Which structure carries neural impulses from the eye to the brain?
wrong: The corpus callosum between the hemispheres
Optic nerve.exp: The optic nerve carries visual signals to the brain.

Primary visual cortex.q: Where in the brain is visual input first processed?
wrong: In the primary auditory cortex of the temporal lobe
Primary visual cortex.exp: The primary visual cortex is in the occipital lobe.

Feature detectors.q: Some neurons in your visual cortex fire only when you see a line at a certain angle. What are they?
wrong: Bipolar cells in the retina at the back of the eye
Those are in the retina, not the cortex.
Those relay signals in the CNS.
Feature detectors.exp: They respond to specific features like shape, angle or movement.

Parallel processing.q: When you see a bird fly by, your brain handles its color, motion and shape at the same time, then combines them. What is this?
wrong: Transduction of light energy in the retina
Transduction converts energy; this is combining features.
Parallel processing.exp: Processing many aspects of a stimulus at once.

Trichromatic theory.q: Which theory explains color at the level of the retina, using red, green and blue receptors?
wrong: That explains color in the brain and afterimages.

Color blindness.q: A boy can't tell red from green on a traffic light. What is the most likely cause?
wrong: Damaged rods that handle vision in dim light
Color blindness.exp: Color blindness usually comes from impaired red or green cones.

Opponent-process theory.q: Which theory says color is processed in the brain by pairs like red/green and yellow/blue?
wrong: Trichromatic theory of three types of cones
That explains the retina, not opposing pairs.
Opponent-process theory.exp: A cell can signal only one color of each pair at a time.

Afterimage.q: You stare at a green square for a minute, then look at a white wall and see a red square. What is this?
wrong: That is a feeling in an amputated limb.

Which color theory is right?.q: A classmate says the trichromatic and opponent-process theories can't both be right. What is the best reply?
Which color theory is right?.right: Both are right, at different stages
wrong: Only trichromatic theory, since it came first
Both theories explain part of color vision.
Neither; color is processed in the ear
Which color theory is right?.exp: Trichromatic explains the retina; opponent-process explains the brain.

Gestalt.q: You look at a few curved lines and instantly see a smiley face. What idea does this show?
wrong: Feature detection of single lines and angles
You see the whole, not separate features.
That converts energy into neural signals.
Gestalt.exp: We combine pieces into meaningful wholes.

Proximity.q: You see "XX XX XX" as three pairs rather than six X's. Which Gestalt principle is at work?
wrong: Similarity, grouping things that look alike
All the X's look alike; spacing is what groups them.
That is separating objects from background.
Proximity.exp: We group objects that are close together.

Similarity.q: In a grid of dots, you see rows because every other row is red. Which principle is this?
wrong: Proximity, grouping things that are close
The spacing is even; color does the grouping.
Similarity.exp: We group objects that look alike.

Closure.q: A circle drawn with small gaps still looks like a complete circle to you. Which principle explains this?
wrong: That is about objects standing out.
Closure.exp: We fill in gaps to see a complete shape.

Figure-ground.q: In the famous vase/faces picture, you can see either a vase or two faces depending on what stands out. Which principle?
wrong: Closure, filling in gaps in a shape
There are no gaps to fill.
That is grouping things that look alike.
Figure-ground.exp: Organizing a scene into a figure and its ground.

Depth perception.q: A baby refuses to crawl onto glass covering a drop-off. Which ability is the baby using?
wrong: Sensory interaction between taste and smell
That is one sense affecting another.
Depth perception.exp: Judging how far away things are.

Binocular cues.q: A person who loses an eye has trouble judging the distance of a ball tossed to them. Which cues did they lose?
wrong: Monocular cues, which work with one eye
Monocular cues still work with one eye.

Retinal disparity.q: Hold a finger close to your face and close each eye in turn: it seems to jump. What depth cue does this show?
wrong: Linear perspective, lines meeting in the distance
That is about one object blocking another.
Retinal disparity.exp: Each eye gets a slightly different image; a bigger difference means closer.

Monocular cues.q: Painters show depth on a flat canvas using cues that work with just one eye. What are these called?
wrong: Binocular cues, which need both eyes
A flat painting can't use both-eye cues.

Relative size.q: Two people who are really the same height appear in a photo, and one looks much smaller. Which cue makes that one seem farther away?
wrong: Interposition, where one object blocks another
Relative size.exp: If two objects are assumed the same size, the smaller-looking one seems farther.

Interposition.q: A tree partly blocks your view of a house. Which cue tells you the tree is closer?
wrong: Linear perspective, parallel lines that converge
Interposition.exp: An object blocking another is seen as closer.

Linear perspective.q: Train tracks seem to meet in the distance. Which depth cue is this?
wrong: Relative clarity, where hazy things look far away
That is about haze, not converging lines.
Linear perspective.exp: Parallel lines seem to converge in the distance.

Relative clarity.q: On a foggy day, the hazy mountains seem farther away than they really are. Which cue explains this?
wrong: Retinal disparity between the two eyes' images
That is a Gestalt grouping principle.
Relative clarity.exp: Sharp objects seem closer; hazy ones seem farther.

Audition.q: Which sense is studied when researchers test how well people hear different pitches?

Amplitude.q: You turn up the volume on your speaker. Which property of the sound wave increases?
wrong: Frequency, which sets how high the pitch is

Frequency.q: A singer goes from a low note to a high note. Which property of the sound wave increased?
wrong: Amplitude, the height of the sound wave
That is telling where a sound comes from.

Sound localization.q: A car honks to your right, and you instantly know which side it's on. How?
Sound localization.right: Your right ear hears it slightly louder and sooner
wrong: Your left ear hears it louder because sound crosses over
The nearer ear hears it louder and sooner.
Your eyes tell your ears where to listen
Only the cochlea in the right ear detects it
Both ears hear it; the difference tells direction.
Sound localization.exp: The nearer ear hears it slightly louder and slightly sooner.

Eardrum.q: Which membrane between the outer and middle ear vibrates when sound waves hit it?
wrong: The cochlea, the snail-shaped inner ear tube
The cochlea is in the inner ear.

Ossicles.q: Which three tiny bones of the middle ear pass vibrations from the eardrum to the cochlea?
wrong: The semicircular canals of the vestibular sense

Cochlea.q: In which fluid-filled, snail-shaped tube do hair cells turn vibrations into neural signals?
wrong: The eardrum between the outer and middle ear
The eardrum vibrates; it doesn't contain hair cells.
Cochlea.exp: Transduction for hearing happens in the cochlea.

Conduction hearing loss.q: A child's hearing loss comes from damaged middle-ear bones and can be fixed with surgery. What type is it?
wrong: Sensorineural hearing loss from damaged hair cells
That is one sense triggering another.

Sensorineural hearing loss.q: Years of loud concerts destroy hair cells in a musician's cochlea. What type of hearing loss results?
wrong: Conduction hearing loss that surgery can repair
Hair-cell damage isn't conduction loss and can't be reversed.
That is one sense triggering another.
Sensorineural hearing loss.exp: Nerve deafness: damage to the hair cells or auditory nerve.

Cochlear implant.q: Which device can help a person with sensorineural hearing loss by sending electrical signals up the auditory nerve?
wrong: A hearing aid that simply makes sounds louder for the ear
A cochlear implant bypasses damaged hair cells.
Cochlear implant.exp: It turns sounds into electrical signals sent up the auditory nerve.

Vestibular sense.q: After spinning on a playground ride, you stop but still feel dizzy. Which sense explains this?
wrong: Kinesthesis, the sense of body part position
Kinesthesis senses body parts, not head balance.
Vestibular sense.exp: Fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving after you stop.

Kinesthesis.q: With your eyes closed, you can still touch your nose with your finger. Which sense makes this possible?
wrong: The vestibular sense of balance in the inner ear
That senses head position and balance.
Kinesthesis.exp: Sensors in muscles, tendons and joints track body parts.

Olfaction.q: The smell of a certain perfume instantly brings back an emotional memory. Why might smell do this more than other senses?
Olfaction.right: Smell skips the thalamus for limbic areas
wrong: Smell is processed only in the occipital lobe with vision
Smell receptors are in the tongue
They are in the nasal cavity.
Smell travels through the optic nerve
Olfaction.exp: Olfaction goes to areas connected to the limbic system.

Gustation.q: You burn your tongue on hot soup, but a couple of weeks later your taste is back to normal. Why?
Gustation.right: Taste buds regenerate about every two weeks
wrong: Your olfactory receptors take over the work of tasting
Smell helps taste, but your taste buds recover.
Taste is controlled by the cochlea
Gustation.exp: Taste buds regenerate about every two weeks.

Five basic tastes.q: A savory broth tastes rich and meaty. Which basic taste is this?
Five basic tastes.exp: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami (savory).

Supertasters.q: Lucas finds jalapeños unbearably hot while his friends barely notice. What might explain this?
wrong: He has sensorineural hearing loss affecting his taste
He has fewer taste buds than average
Fewer taste buds would weaken taste.
Supertasters.exp: Supertasters have more taste buds and feel taste and pain more intensely.

Sensory interaction.q: You hold your nose while taking bad-tasting medicine, and it tastes less awful. What does this show?
wrong: Synesthesia, where senses trigger one another
Synesthesia is one sense triggering a different experience, like seeing colors.

Touch.q: Which four skin senses combine to make up the sense of touch?
wrong: Rods, cones, bipolar and ganglion cells
Touch.exp: Touch = pressure, warmth, cold and pain.

Gate control theory.q: A child bumps her knee, then rubs it and is distracted by a toy, and the pain fades. Which theory explains this?
wrong: That explains color at the retina.
Gate control theory.exp: Distraction can close the spinal cord's pain gate.

Phantom limb.q: Months after losing his leg, a veteran still feels it itch. What explains this?
wrong: Synesthesia, one sense triggering another sense
There is no limb to sense.
Phantom limb.exp: The sensory cortex area for the limb is still active.

Synesthesia.q: Every time Mia hears a trumpet, she sees the color orange. What is this?
wrong: Sensory interaction like smell changing taste
That is one sense changing another, not triggering a new experience.
That follows staring at a color.

Prosopagnosia.q: A man can describe a face in detail but can't recognize his own brother. What condition is this?

Sleep.q: A classmate says your brain "turns off" when you sleep. What is the best correction?
Sleep.right: Sleep is an altered state; the brain stays active
wrong: The brain does turn off completely, but only in deep sleep
Even in deep sleep the brain is active.
Only the body sleeps; the mind is fully awake
Sleep is an altered state of consciousness.
Sleep is the same as being unconscious from a coma
A coma is different from sleep.
Sleep.exp: Even sound asleep, your brain is still active.

Dreaming.q: A friend insists she never dreams. What does your class say?
wrong: Only people who sleep more than 8 hours ever dream
Dreaming.exp: She dreams; she just doesn't remember.

Sleep stages.q: Which list shows the four stages of sleep?
wrong: Alpha, beta, gamma and delta stages of waking life
Those are not the stages on your slides.
There are three NREM stages and one REM.

Circadian rhythm.q: After flying across the world, a traveler feels wide awake at 3 a.m. What has been thrown off?
wrong: Her refractory period between neural firings
That is about neurons, not the 24-hour cycle.

Body temperature cycle.q: When is body temperature usually lowest?
wrong: Right after lunch, when it peaks for the day
It dips in the afternoon; it's lowest at night.
It is still higher than at night.
Body temperature cycle.exp: Temperature rises through the day, dips in the afternoon and is lowest at night.

Teens and young adults.q: A school moves the hardest test from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Why might this help most teens?
Teens and young adults.right: Teens tend to do better later in the day
wrong: Teens are most alert early in the morning, before school
Teens' body temperature is highest at night
Teens and young adults.exp: Most teens and young adults are evening-energized.

Older adults.q: Grandpa is sharpest at 7 a.m. and fading by evening. What does this pattern match?
Older adults.right: Older adults tend to be morning people
wrong: Teens and young adults, who are evening-energized
That is being unable to sleep.
Older adults.exp: Most older adults' energy declines as the day goes on.

Artificial light.q: Ana scrolls her phone in bed for an hour and then can't fall asleep. What might be interfering?
wrong: Too much leptin from a big dinner earlier that night
Leptin signals fullness; the screen light is the issue.
Artificial light.exp: Artificial light can interfere with circadian rhythms.

Sleep loss: brain.q: A student pulls all-nighters before tests and remembers less of what she studied. Which effect of sleep loss is this?
wrong: A lower risk of developing depression later in life
Sleep loss raises the risk of depression.
Sleep loss: brain.exp: Sleep loss reduces focus and memory consolidation and raises the risk of depression.

Sleep loss: immune system.q: During finals week with little sleep, Tom keeps catching colds. Why?
Sleep loss: immune system.right: Sleep loss suppresses his immune system
wrong: Sleep loss lowers his ghrelin and makes him less hungry
Sleep loss raises ghrelin, and that's about hunger.
Sleep loss raises the risk of viral infections.
Sleep loss: immune system.exp: Fewer immune cells, more viral infections.

Sleep loss: stomach and fat cells.q: Why do people who sleep too little often gain weight?
wrong: Less ghrelin and more leptin, so they feel full all day
It's the reverse: more hunger, less fullness.
Sleep loss: stomach and fat cells.exp: More hunger-arousing ghrelin, less hunger-suppressing leptin, more fat cells.

Sleep loss: heart.q: Which heart-related risk rises with chronic sleep loss?
wrong: A slower and healthier resting heart rate
Sleep loss isn't good for the heart.
Sleep loss: heart.exp: Sleep loss increases the risk of high blood pressure.

Sleep loss: muscles and joints.q: A tired athlete reacts slowly and learns new moves poorly. Which effect of sleep loss is this?
wrong: Less joint inflammation and stronger muscles overall
Sleep loss increases inflammation and reduces strength.
Sleep loss: muscles and joints.exp: Reduced strength, slower reaction time and motor learning, more inflammation.

Insomnia.q: For months, Rosa lies awake for hours every night unable to sleep. Which disorder fits?
wrong: Narcolepsy, which causes sudden sleep attacks
That is stopping breathing during sleep.
Those are episodes of terror in Stage 3.

Sleep apnea.q: A man snores loudly, stops breathing for moments during the night, and wakes up exhausted. Which disorder fits?
wrong: Insomnia, trouble falling or staying asleep
Insomnia is being unable to sleep.

Night terrors.q: A child wakes up screaming in Stage 3 sleep but has no memory of it the next morning. What is this?
wrong: A nightmare remembered from REM sleep
Night terrors are not nightmares and aren't remembered.
Night terrors.exp: Intense fear with no recollection, in Stage 3.

Sleepwalking.q: A teenager is found in the kitchen at night, eyes open but asleep. Which sleep disorder is this?
wrong: Narcolepsy, falling asleep during the day
She is asleep, not unable to sleep.

Narcolepsy.q: A man suddenly falls asleep in the middle of conversations during the day. Which disorder fits?
wrong: Insomnia, being unable to sleep at night
That is about breathing during sleep.

Psychoactive drugs.q: Chemicals that change how people perceive and feel by affecting neurotransmitters at the synapse are called what?
wrong: Hormones released by the endocrine glands
Psychoactive drugs.exp: Psychoactive drugs alter perceptions and mood.

Agonist.q: A drug fits into endorphin receptors and mimics endorphins, increasing their effects. What kind of drug is it?
wrong: An antagonist that blocks the neurotransmitter
This describes how it acts at receptors.
A placebo has no chemical effect.
Agonist.exp: Agonist = acts like it (opiates and endorphins).

Antagonist.q: A drug blocks the effects of a neurotransmitter instead of mimicking it. What kind of drug is it?
wrong: An agonist that mimics the neurotransmitter

Reuptake inhibitor.q: Cocaine keeps dopamine from being reabsorbed, so it stays in the synapse. What is this action called?
wrong: Agonism, mimicking the neurotransmitter at receptors
Cocaine blocks reabsorption rather than mimicking dopamine.

Four categories of psychoactive drugs.q: Which list names the four categories of psychoactive drugs?
wrong: Agonists, antagonists, reuptake inhibitors, placebos, sedatives
Those describe how drugs act, not the categories.
Not the names on your slides.

Depressants.q: Which category of drugs slows you down by reducing neural activity?
wrong: Stimulants, which excite the nervous system

Alcohol.q: People act wild when drinking, so many think alcohol is a stimulant. What is it really?
wrong: A stimulant that raises dopamine and glutamate
Alcohol reduces glutamate and calms the nervous system.
It doesn't come from the opium poppy.
Alcohol.exp: Alcohol intensifies GABA and reduces glutamate.

Barbiturates / sedatives.q: A doctor prescribes "downers" for insomnia that increase GABA, with effects similar to alcohol. What are they?
Barbiturates / sedatives.exp: Downers that increase GABA; they can cause dependence.

Benzodiazepines.q: Xanax and Valium are prescribed to calm anxiety. Which drug group are they?
wrong: Amphetamines that boost alertness and energy
Those come from the opium poppy.

Stimulants.q: Which category of drugs excites the central nervous system?

Caffeine.q: After four energy drinks, Max feels anxious, his heart races and he can't sleep. Which drug's high dose explains this?
wrong: Alcohol, a depressant that calms the system
Caffeine.exp: High doses of caffeine cause anxiety, palpitations and insomnia.

Nicotine.q: A smoker who quits becomes irritable, nervous and gets headaches. Which drug is he withdrawing from?
wrong: LSD, a hallucinogen that distorts perception
LSD isn't smoked like this and isn't known for these withdrawal symptoms.

Cocaine.q: A drug gives a burst of euphoria by blocking dopamine reabsorption, then a crash with depression and strong cravings. Which drug?
wrong: Alcohol, which increases the effects of GABA
Cocaine.exp: Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake, then crashes.

Amphetamines.q: A drug mimics adrenaline, causing alertness and euphoria followed by a huge crash. Meth is one form. Which group?
wrong: Benzodiazepines, which calm the nervous system

Hallucinogens.q: Which category of drugs distorts what you see and hear?
wrong: Depressants, which slow down the nervous system

LSD.q: A drug produces hallucinations and delusions, like a psychotic state, and can lead to paranoia. Which drug?
wrong: Caffeine in very high doses from energy drinks
Caffeine causes anxiety and insomnia, not hallucinations.

THC.q: The active ingredient in marijuana can cause mild hallucinations, relaxation and a distorted sense of time. What is it?

Ecstasy (MDMA).q: Which drug is both a stimulant and a hallucinogen and can damage serotonin-producing neurons?
wrong: LSD, a hallucinogen that is not a stimulant
Ecstasy (MDMA).exp: MDMA can cause lasting mood and memory problems.

Opioids.q: Heroin, codeine, morphine and oxycodone all belong to which category?
wrong: They don't excite the nervous system.
Opioids.exp: Opioids come from the opium poppy.

How opioids work.q: Why do long-term opioid users feel awful without the drug?
How opioids work.right: The brain stops making endorphins and dopamine
wrong: Opioids permanently block serotonin receptors in the gut
Opioids are antagonists that block pain signals
How opioids work.exp: Opioids act as endorphin agonists; with continued use the brain stops producing its own.

Results of opioid use.q: Which list shows results of opioid use on your slides?
wrong: Better memory, stronger immune system, more energy, focus
These aren't results of opioid use.
Results of opioid use.exp: Opioid use leads to dependence, tolerance, withdrawal and addiction.

Substance use.q: Jen has a glass of wine at family dinners, and it never affects her work or life. How would your slides describe this?
wrong: Substance abuse that disrupts daily functioning
Her use doesn't interfere with her life.
She doesn't crave it despite consequences.
Substance use.exp: Use that doesn't interfere with daily functioning.

Substance abuse.q: Kyle's drinking makes him miss work, drive dangerously and get arrested. How would your slides describe this?
wrong: Substance use that doesn't interfere with life
That is needing more for the same effect.
Substance abuse.exp: A pattern that hurts functioning, causes danger and legal trouble.

Tolerance.q: A coffee drinker now needs three cups to feel the buzz one cup used to give. What is this?
wrong: Withdrawal, the distress after stopping a drug
Tolerance can be part of addiction, but this is tolerance.
Tolerance.exp: Needing larger amounts for the same effect.

Addiction.q: Sam keeps using a drug he no longer enjoys, even after losing friends over it, because he craves it. What is this?
wrong: Tolerance, needing more for the same effect
Tolerance alone doesn't mean craving despite consequences.
Addiction.exp: Craving and using despite consequences: wanting it more than liking it.

Withdrawal.q: After quitting caffeine, Lily gets headaches and feels miserable for a week. What is she experiencing?
wrong: Tolerance, needing more for the same effect
Tolerance is about needing more, not stopping.
Withdrawal.exp: Discomfort and distress after stopping an addictive drug.

Substance use disorder.q: A doctor uses 11 DSM-5 criteria to decide whether a patient's drinking is a disorder. What is she diagnosing?
wrong: Generalized anxiety disorder from constant worry
Substance use disorder.exp: Craving and use despite life disruption or risk; 11 criteria.

Severity levels.q: A patient meets 5 of the 11 criteria for substance use disorder. How severe is it, per your slide?
wrong: Mild, which is three criteria met
Severity levels.exp: Mild = 3, moderate = 4 or 5, severe = 6 or more.

Criteria: losing control.q: Dan keeps drinking more than he planned and fails every time he tries to cut back. Which group of criteria is this?
wrong: Risk and the body, like tolerance and withdrawal
Those are about danger and the body.
Those are about work, school and relationships.
Criteria: losing control.exp: Using more or longer than intended and failing to cut down.

Criteria: life problems.q: Alicia quits her soccer team and skips school because of her drug use. Which group of criteria is this?
wrong: Losing control over how much is used
That is about amounts and failing to cut down.
That is about danger and physical effects.
That is one criterion about the body.
Criteria: life problems.exp: Failing duties and giving up important activities.

Criteria: risk and the body.q: Ray keeps using even though it worsened his heart condition, and he now needs more to feel anything. Which group of criteria is this?
wrong: Life problems at work, home and school
Those are about responsibilities and relationships.
That is about amounts and failing to cut down.
Criteria: risk and the body.exp: Continuing despite physical harm, plus tolerance and withdrawal.

Split-brain patient.q: Surgeons cut a patient's corpus callosum to stop severe seizures. What happens to her two hemispheres?
Split-brain patient.right: They can no longer share information
wrong: They merge into a single hemisphere that controls everything
They stay separate; they just can't communicate.
Split-brain patient.exp: Split-brain: the hemispheres can't share information.

Left visual field (LVF).q: Everything to the left of where you're looking goes to which hemisphere?
wrong: The left hemisphere, the language side of the brain
Visual fields cross: left field goes to the right brain.
Each field goes to the opposite side.
Neither; it goes to the cerebellum

Right visual field (RVF).q: Everything to the right of where you're looking goes to which hemisphere?
wrong: The right hemisphere, the face-recognition side
Visual fields cross: right field goes to the left brain.
Each field goes to the opposite side.
Right visual field (RVF).exp: Right field → left brain, the language side.

Optic chiasm.q: At which X-shaped point do the optic nerves cross, so each visual field reaches the opposite hemisphere?
wrong: The corpus callosum between the two hemispheres
That connects the hemispheres, not the optic nerves.

Object flashed to the right visual field.q: A split-brain patient sees the word "key" flashed in her right visual field. What can she do?
wrong: Point to the key with her left hand but not name it
That happens with the left visual field.
That happens with the left visual field.
The left hemisphere can name it.
Object flashed to the right visual field.exp: The right field reaches the left hemisphere, which can speak.

Object flashed to the left visual field.q: A split-brain patient sees a picture of a spoon in her left visual field. What happens?
Object flashed to the left visual field.right: She says "nothing" but points with her left hand
wrong: She names the spoon out loud right away
She points to it with her right hand and then names it
The right hand is controlled by the left hemisphere.
She can't respond in any way
Her left hand can point to it.
Object flashed to the left visual field.exp: Left field → right hemisphere → left hand, no words.

Trees vs. forest.q: Looking at a painting, one hemisphere notices the tiny brushstrokes and the other sees the whole scene. Which sees the whole scene?
wrong: The left hemisphere, which focuses on small details
The left focuses on details (the trees).
Neither; only the occipital lobe sees

Words vs. tone.q: Your friend says "Great job" sarcastically. Which hemisphere picks up on the sarcastic tone?
wrong: The left hemisphere, which handles literal word meanings
The left handles the words' literal meaning.

Logic vs. intuition.q: Solving a step-by-step math proof relies most on which hemisphere's style?
wrong: The right hemisphere, with feelings and intuition
The right handles intuition and perception.
Logic vs. intuition.exp: Left = logic, linear thinking and calculation.
